chapter_text:
CHAPTER 1 — ANCIENT WORLD

Introduction

When does 'history' begin? The story of humanity stretches across many tens of thousands of years, but the period historians call the ANCIENT WORLD runs roughly from the development of agriculture and the first settled societies (around 10 000 years ago) down to about the 5th century CE, when several great empires — Roman in the west, Gupta in India — gave way to the medieval period. This chapter sketches that long arc: the Stone Age, the Bronze and Iron Ages, the rise of the great river-valley civilisations, the classical empires of Greece and Rome, and the parallel development of Persian, Chinese and Indian civilisations. We end with a focus on India's enormous contributions to mathematics, science, art and religion.

1.1 PREHISTORIC AGES

Before writing, before metals, humans lived as hunter-gatherers. Tools at first were rough stones — the OLD STONE AGE (Palaeolithic, ~2.5 million BCE to 10 000 BCE). Then came the MIDDLE STONE AGE (Mesolithic) and the NEW STONE AGE (Neolithic, beginning ~10 000 BCE), in which polished stone tools, agriculture, animal domestication, pottery and the first permanent villages appeared. The Neolithic revolution was probably the single biggest change in human history — it created the surplus that made cities, kings, writing and civilisation itself possible.

Three successive 'metal ages' followed:
 - COPPER AGE (Chalcolithic): use of pure copper alongside stone.
 - BRONZE AGE (~3300-1200 BCE): copper alloyed with tin — bronze — gave better tools and weapons. River-valley civilisations of Egypt, Mesopotamia, the Indus and China flourished in this period.
 - IRON AGE (~1200 BCE onward): iron is harder, more plentiful and cheaper than bronze. Its spread transformed society — farms expanded, armies grew, large kingdoms became possible.

1.2 RIVER-VALLEY CIVILISATIONS

The first civilisations grew on the banks of great rivers because farming was easy in fertile flood-plains and water transport linked towns together. Four classic examples:
 - EGYPT — along the Nile. Pyramids, hieroglyphics, pharaohs, ~3100 BCE.
 - MESOPOTAMIA — between the Tigris and the Euphrates (modern Iraq). Sumerian city-states, cuneiform writing, the Epic of Gilgamesh, the wheel.
 - INDUS VALLEY (Harappan) — along the Indus and its tributaries (modern Pakistan + north-west India). Planned cities like Mohenjo-Daro and Harappa, sophisticated drainage, the Great Bath. ~2600-1900 BCE.
 - CHINA — along the Yellow River (Huang He). Shang dynasty, oracle bones, early Chinese writing.

These civilisations independently invented writing — a precondition for the kind of complex administration that empires need.

1.3 GREECE — THE CLASSICAL POLIS

From about 800 BCE the city-states (POLEIS) of Greece — Athens, Sparta, Corinth and many others — grew into independent political units. Athens experimented with DEMOCRACY (around 500 BCE) — citizens (a limited definition: free adult males) voted on laws and held public office. The Greeks invented or refined philosophy (Socrates, Plato, Aristotle), drama (Sophocles, Euripides), history (Herodotus, Thucydides), mathematics (Pythagoras, Euclid), and science (Archimedes, Hippocrates). Greek art and architecture — the Parthenon, marble sculpture — set canonical standards. Alexander the Great (356-323 BCE) carried Greek culture as far east as the Indus.

1.4 ROME — REPUBLIC AND EMPIRE

Rome began as a small Italian town (traditional founding date 753 BCE), grew into a REPUBLIC governed by elected magistrates and a Senate, and after the civil wars of the 1st century BCE became an EMPIRE under Augustus (27 BCE). At its height (2nd century CE) the Roman Empire stretched from Britain to the Persian Gulf, containing perhaps 50-60 million people. Roman law (the basis of much modern European law), engineering (aqueducts, roads, concrete), and Latin language profoundly shaped the West. Christianity began as a small Jewish sect in Roman Judea around 30 CE and within four centuries was the official religion of the Empire.

1.5 PERSIA AND THE NEAR EAST

The Achaemenid Persian Empire (550-330 BCE), founded by Cyrus the Great, was the largest empire of the ancient world before Rome — stretching from Greece to the Indus. The Persians developed efficient road systems, postal networks, multi-ethnic administration, and Zoroastrianism (one of the earliest monotheistic-leaning religions, founded by Zarathustra). Persia influenced Greek thought and was conquered by Alexander.

1.6 ANCIENT INDIA — VEDIC TO MAURYA

In India the Indus Valley Civilisation declined around 1900 BCE; from about 1500 BCE the VEDIC age unfolded — a long period of oral composition of the Vedas (Rigveda, Samaveda, Yajurveda, Atharvaveda), the development of Sanskrit, and the gradual settlement of the Indo-Gangetic plain. By the 6th century BCE the IRON AGE had reshaped Indian society: surplus, kingdoms (mahajanapadas), trade and questioning intellectual movements.

 - JAINISM (founded by Mahavira, 6th century BCE) emphasised non-violence (ahimsa), austerity, and respect for all living beings.
 - BUDDHISM (founded by Gautama Buddha around the same time) taught the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path, rejecting ritual and caste.
Both were 'reformatory' movements responding to the elaborate ritualism of Vedic Brahmanism.

The MAURYAN EMPIRE (322-185 BCE), founded by Chandragupta Maurya and reaching its peak under ASHOKA (~268-232 BCE), united most of the subcontinent under a single administration for the first time. Ashoka's conversion to Buddhism after the Kalinga war, and his edicts carved on rocks and pillars across India, remain monuments of early Indian governance.

Later the GUPTA EMPIRE (320-550 CE) ushered in what is sometimes called the 'classical age' of India: peace, prosperity, and remarkable cultural and scientific achievement.

1.7 INDIA'S CONTRIBUTIONS TO HUMAN CIVILISATION

India made foundational contributions in many fields:
 - MATHEMATICS — concept of zero and place-value decimal system (Aryabhata, Brahmagupta); 'Arabic' numerals are actually Indian; Aryabhata's value of π and his sine tables.
 - ASTRONOMY — Aryabhata's heliocentric hints; Varahamihira's compilations.
 - MEDICINE — Charaka Samhita and Sushruta Samhita; Ayurveda; ancient surgical techniques including plastic surgery.
 - METALLURGY — the Iron Pillar of Delhi (rust-resistant for over 1600 years).
 - PHILOSOPHY — the six classical schools (Sankhya, Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Mimamsa, Vedanta); Upanishads.
 - ART AND ARCHITECTURE — temple architecture, cave temples of Ajanta and Ellora, the stupas of Sanchi.
 - LITERATURE — Mahabharata, Ramayana, the works of Kalidasa, Panini's Sanskrit grammar.

SUMMARY

- Prehistoric humans moved from the Old Stone Age through Mesolithic, Neolithic, Copper, Bronze and Iron Ages — each driven by tool-and-technique innovations.
- The Neolithic revolution (~10 000 BCE) introduced agriculture, settled villages and pottery.
- The Bronze and Iron Ages brought river-valley civilisations: Egypt, Mesopotamia, the Indus Valley, China.
- Classical Greece invented philosophy, drama and an early form of democracy.
- Rome, beginning as a city-state, built a republic and then an empire that stretched across the Mediterranean.
- Persia, China and India each developed parallel civilisations with their own contributions.
- In India: Indus Valley → Vedic age → mahajanapadas → Mauryan and Gupta empires; the 6th century BCE saw the rise of Buddhism and Jainism.
- Indian contributions to world civilisation include the decimal place-value system, zero, advances in astronomy, medicine, metallurgy, philosophy, art and literature.

chapter_summary.title: Ancient World — Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Class 10 Social Science (213) summary for Lesson 1. It surveys the long arc of human history from prehistoric hunter-gatherers through the metal ages, the four river-valley civilisations, classical Greece, Rome and Persia, and the parallel development of Vedic India, the Mauryan empire under Ashoka, the Gupta classical age, and India's lasting contributions to world civilisation.

sections.heading: Prehistoric and metal ages
bullets: The Old Stone Age (Palaeolithic), Middle Stone Age (Mesolithic) and New Stone Age (Neolithic) trace the development of stone tools.
The Neolithic revolution introduced agriculture, animal domestication, pottery and the first permanent villages — laying the foundations of all later civilisation.
The Bronze Age (~3300-1200 BCE) saw the rise of the great river-valley civilisations.
The Iron Age (~1200 BCE onward) brought radical changes in social and economic life across different countries at different times — farms expanded, kingdoms grew.

sections.heading: River-valley civilisations
bullets: Egypt arose on the Nile — pyramids, pharaohs, hieroglyphics, organised state by 3100 BCE.
Mesopotamia (Sumer, Babylon, Assyria) developed between the Tigris and the Euphrates — cuneiform writing, the wheel, the first cities.
The Indus Valley Civilisation flourished from 2600-1900 BCE — Mohenjo-Daro, Harappa, planned cities with sophisticated drainage.
Ancient China grew along the Yellow River — Shang dynasty, oracle bones, early writing.
All four invented writing independently — a precondition for complex administration and history.

sections.heading: Greece and Rome
bullets: Greek city-states (Athens, Sparta, Corinth) developed independent political life from ~800 BCE; Athens experimented with democracy around 500 BCE.
Greek contributions: philosophy (Socrates, Plato, Aristotle); drama (Sophocles); science (Archimedes, Pythagoras); art and architecture (the Parthenon).
Rome grew from a city-state (753 BCE) to a Republic, then an Empire under Augustus (27 BCE); at its height ruled ~50-60 million people.
Roman contributions: law (basis of much European law), engineering (aqueducts, roads), Latin language; later, Christianity became the official religion.

sections.heading: Persia and ancient India
bullets: The Achaemenid Persian Empire (550-330 BCE) was the largest empire of the ancient world before Rome; introduced efficient road and postal systems and a multi-ethnic administration.
India: Indus Valley declined ~1900 BCE; Vedic age (1500 BCE onward) saw the composition of the Vedas and the spread of Sanskrit.
Buddhism and Jainism were the first reformatory movements in 6th century BCE India.
The Mauryan empire (322-185 BCE) under Chandragupta and Ashoka united most of the subcontinent; the Gupta empire (320-550 CE) ushered in India's classical age.

sections.heading: India's contributions to civilisation
bullets: India has made tremendous contributions in the fields of mathematics, astronomy, chemistry, metallurgy, medicines, art, architecture, literature and learning.
The decimal place-value system and the concept of zero originated in India (Aryabhata, Brahmagupta) and spread through the Islamic world to Europe as 'Arabic numerals'.
Ayurveda, with the Charaka Samhita and Sushruta Samhita as foundational texts, included surgical techniques (Sushruta is sometimes called the father of plastic surgery).
The Iron Pillar of Delhi has stood for over 1600 years without rusting — a testament to early Indian metallurgy.
Classical Indian literature includes the Mahabharata, the Ramayana, the plays and poems of Kalidasa, and Panini's grammar of Sanskrit.

key_takeaways: The Neolithic revolution (~10 000 BCE) introduced agriculture and settled life — the precondition for all later civilisation.
The Iron Age brought radical changes in social and economic life at different times in different countries.
Four classic river-valley civilisations — Egypt, Mesopotamia, Indus, China — independently invented urban life and writing.
Greeks, Romans, Persians and Indians made significant contributions in polity, philosophy, art, architecture and sculpture.
In 6th century BCE India, Buddhism and Jainism arose as the first reformatory movements.
Indian civilisation made tremendous contributions in mathematics (especially zero), astronomy, medicine, metallurgy, art, architecture and literature.

glossary.definition: The earliest period of human prehistory characterised by rough stone tools and a hunter-gatherer lifestyle.
The later Stone Age in which polished stone tools, agriculture, animal domestication, pottery and permanent villages appeared.
The period in which copper alloyed with tin (bronze) was the principal material for tools and weapons; saw the rise of the river-valley civilisations.
The period beginning ~1200 BCE in which iron tools became dominant, transforming agriculture, warfare and social organisation.
An early civilisation that arose along a fertile river — examples: Egypt on the Nile, Mesopotamia on the Tigris-Euphrates, the Indus Valley, and China on the Yellow River.
An ancient Greek city-state — an independent political unit comprising a city and its surrounding territory.
A system of government in which citizens choose leaders or vote on laws. Athens experimented with direct democracy around 500 BCE for free adult male citizens.
The pre-imperial Roman government (509-27 BCE), in which elected magistrates and the Senate held authority.
The Roman state from 27 BCE under Augustus; at its height ruled most of the Mediterranean world.
The period in ancient India (~1500-500 BCE) during which the Vedas were composed and Sanskrit developed.
Sixteen major kingdoms and oligarchic republics in northern India in the 6th century BCE.
The first empire to unite most of the Indian subcontinent (322-185 BCE), reaching its peak under Ashoka.
An Indian empire (320-550 CE) often called the 'classical age' of India for its cultural and scientific achievement.
A reformatory movement founded by Gautama Buddha in 6th century BCE India; teaches the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path.
A reformatory movement founded by Mahavira (6th century BCE); emphasises non-violence (ahimsa), austerity and respect for all living beings.

worksheet.title: Worksheet — Ancient World
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Each question is followed by its marks. Answers to numerical / dating questions should cite the correct period or empire.

questions.question: What was the Neolithic revolution, and why is it considered a turning point in human history?
questions.answer: The Neolithic revolution was the transition from a hunter-gatherer lifestyle to settled agriculture, around 10 000 BCE. People domesticated plants and animals, made polished stone tools and pottery, and built the first permanent villages. It was a turning point because the resulting food surplus made cities, kings, writing, organised religion, trade and ultimately all of civilisation possible.

questions.question: Name the four classic river-valley civilisations and the rivers along which each grew.
questions.answer: Egyptian civilisation along the Nile; Mesopotamian civilisation between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers; Indus Valley (Harappan) civilisation along the Indus and its tributaries; ancient Chinese civilisation along the Yellow River (Huang He).

questions.question: What were the main features of Athenian democracy? Who was eligible to participate?
questions.answer: Athenian democracy (around 500 BCE) was a system in which CITIZENS (a restricted category: free adult males born in Athens) could attend the Assembly, vote on laws, sit on juries and hold public office, often by lot. Women, slaves and resident foreigners (metics) were excluded. It was DIRECT democracy — citizens voted on issues themselves rather than electing representatives. Despite its narrow definition of citizenship, it pioneered ideas of accountability, public deliberation and citizen participation that remain influential today.

questions.question: Trace Rome's political transformation from a city-state to an empire.
questions.answer: Rome was founded as a small city-state on the Italian peninsula (traditional date 753 BCE). It became a REPUBLIC in 509 BCE, governed by elected magistrates and the Senate, with checks and balances. Over the next four centuries Rome expanded across Italy and the Mediterranean. Civil wars in the 1st century BCE destabilised the Republic. Julius Caesar's assassination (44 BCE) was followed by another civil war ending with Octavian — renamed AUGUSTUS — becoming the first emperor in 27 BCE. The EMPIRE then reached its territorial peak in the 2nd century CE before slow decline and division into Western and Eastern halves (the Eastern Roman / Byzantine Empire surviving until 1453 CE).

questions.question: List three major contributions each from Greek and Roman civilisations.
questions.answer:
GREEK contributions: (1) Philosophy — Socrates, Plato, Aristotle laid the foundations of western philosophy. (2) Democracy — direct citizen self-government, first practised in Athens. (3) Science and mathematics — Pythagoras, Euclid, Archimedes; Hippocratic medicine. (Bonus: drama, art, architecture, history-writing.)

ROMAN contributions: (1) Law — Roman law forms the basis of much of European civil law. (2) Engineering — aqueducts, roads, concrete, arches, the Colosseum. (3) Latin language — direct ancestor of all Romance languages (Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese, Romanian).

questions.question: Why are Buddhism and Jainism described as 'reformatory movements' in 6th century BCE India?
questions.answer: By the 6th century BCE, Vedic Brahmanism in India had become heavily ritualistic and rigid — emphasising elaborate sacrifices, priestly authority and the caste system. Buddhism (founded by Gautama Buddha) and Jainism (founded by Mahavira) emerged as critiques of this religious establishment. Both REJECTED elaborate ritual and animal sacrifice; emphasised individual ethical practice (non-violence, truth, meditation); were open to all castes; and addressed questions of human suffering directly (Buddha's Four Noble Truths; Jainism's ahimsa and tapas). Because they reformed and challenged the prevailing religious orthodoxy, historians call them 'reformatory' movements.

questions.question: Briefly describe the achievements of the Mauryan empire under Ashoka.
questions.answer: The Mauryan empire (322-185 BCE), founded by Chandragupta Maurya and reaching its peak under his grandson Ashoka (~268-232 BCE), was the first empire to unite most of the Indian subcontinent. After the bloody KALINGA war (~261 BCE) Ashoka was so disturbed by the suffering caused that he renounced military conquest and converted to BUDDHISM. He spread Buddhist principles of non-violence and ethical living through ROCK AND PILLAR EDICTS (inscriptions placed across the empire), promoted welfare measures (medical care, animal welfare, water supply), and sent Buddhist missionaries as far as Sri Lanka, Burma and the Hellenistic world. Ashoka's reign is remembered as a model of ethical governance.

questions.question: Why is India credited with the invention of zero and the decimal place-value system? Why does it matter?
questions.answer: Indian mathematicians — notably Brahmagupta (7th century CE) — were the first to treat ZERO as a number in its own right (with rules for adding, subtracting and multiplying by it). They also developed the DECIMAL PLACE-VALUE SYSTEM in which the value of a digit depends on its position (so '2' in '23' means 'twenty'). These ideas spread westward through Arab mathematicians (which is why Europeans called them 'Arabic numerals' — though Arabs themselves call them 'Hindu numerals'). Their importance: place-value notation made arithmetic enormously easier than Roman or Greek systems and is the foundation of all modern mathematics, science and engineering. Without zero, neither algebra nor calculus could have developed.

questions.question: Compare the political structure of Athenian democracy with the Mauryan empire under Ashoka. How were citizens governed in each?
questions.answer:
ATHENIAN DEMOCRACY (~500 BCE):
  - Political unit: city-state (polis). Athens had a population of perhaps 250 000 with roughly 30 000 adult male citizens.
  - System: direct democracy. Citizens met in the Assembly, voted on laws, served on juries.
  - Key institutions: the Assembly, the Council of 500 (chosen by lot), elected generals.
  - Limitation: citizenship was restricted to free adult males of Athenian parentage; women, slaves and foreigners were excluded.

MAURYAN EMPIRE under Ashoka (~268-232 BCE):
  - Political unit: vast empire spanning most of the Indian subcontinent — millions of subjects.
  - System: centralised monarchy. The emperor at the top; provincial governors (often royal princes); district officials; village headmen at the base.
  - Key institutions: a sophisticated bureaucracy (described in Kautilya's Arthashastra), an extensive spy network, a large standing army.
  - Distinctive feature under Ashoka: ethical governance based on dharma — rock and pillar edicts promoting non-violence, religious tolerance, and welfare measures.

Comparison: Athens placed governance in the hands of (some) citizens directly; Mauryan India placed all authority in the emperor and his bureaucracy. Both reflect the values and possibilities of their time and place — small polis vs. continental empire required very different political technologies.

questions.explanation: The Harappan script — undeciphered to date.

questions.question: Women had full citizenship rights in Athenian democracy.
questions.explanation: Citizenship was limited to free adult males of Athenian parentage.

questions.question: Pythagoras and Euclid were Greek mathematicians.
questions.explanation: Both made foundational contributions to mathematics.

questions.question: The Achaemenid Persian Empire was larger than the Mauryan empire.
questions.explanation: At their respective peaks; the Achaemenid Empire spanned from Greece to the Indus.

questions.question: Buddhism was founded by Mahavira.
questions.explanation: Mahavira founded Jainism; Gautama Buddha founded Buddhism.

questions.question: Ashoka converted to Buddhism after the Kalinga war.
questions.explanation: Disturbed by the suffering caused, he embraced Buddhism.

questions.question: The concept of zero as a number originated in India.
questions.explanation: Brahmagupta gave rules for arithmetic with zero in the 7th century CE.

questions.question: The Iron Pillar of Delhi is made of pure gold.
questions.explanation: It is made of iron — famous for rust resistance.

questions.question: The Old Stone Age is also called the ____ age.
questions.explanation: From Greek palaios (old) + lithos (stone).

questions.question: Bronze is an alloy of copper and ____.
questions.explanation: Plus minor amounts of other metals in some bronzes.

questions.question: The Egyptian civilisation flourished along the ____ river.
questions.explanation: Egypt is the gift of the Nile.

questions.question: Mesopotamia means 'land between rivers' — the two rivers were the Tigris and the ____.
questions.explanation: Both flow through modern Iraq.

questions.question: The Greek word for a city-state is ____.
questions.explanation: From which 'politics' and 'metropolis' derive.

questions.question: The first Roman emperor was ____ (27 BCE).
questions.explanation: Originally named Octavian.

questions.question: The language of the Romans was ____.
questions.explanation: Ancestor of Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian.

questions.question: The Persian Empire was founded by ____ the Great around 550 BCE.
questions.explanation: He defeated the Medes and unified Persia.

questions.question: The Persian religion founded by Zarathustra is called ____.
questions.explanation: Worship of Ahura Mazda.

questions.question: ____ founded Buddhism in the 6th century BCE.
questions.explanation: Also known as Siddhartha.

questions.question: ____ founded Jainism in the 6th century BCE.
questions.explanation: The 24th Tirthankara.

questions.question: The Mauryan emperor who carved his edicts on rocks and pillars was ____.
questions.explanation: Reigned ~268-232 BCE.

questions.question: The Indian mathematician credited with formalising the rules of zero was ____.
questions.explanation: 7th century CE.

questions.question: The famous Sanskrit grammar by Panini is called the ____.
questions.explanation: Eight chapters describing Sanskrit grammar.

questions.question: The classical age of India is the ____ empire (320-550 CE).
questions.explanation: Peace, prosperity, high cultural achievement.

questions.question: What changes did the Iron Age bring to society?
questions.answer: Iron tools were harder and more plentiful than bronze. With iron axes farmers could clear forests; iron ploughs broke heavier soils. Surplus food allowed bigger settlements and more specialised crafts. Iron weapons gave armies a sharper edge, encouraging the growth of larger kingdoms. The shift to iron occurred at different times in different countries but its social and economic consequences were radical wherever it arrived.

questions.question: Name any four features of the Indus Valley (Harappan) civilisation.
questions.answer: (1) Planned cities with a grid street pattern (Mohenjo-Daro, Harappa). (2) Sophisticated drainage and covered sewers. (3) A pictographic script (still undeciphered). (4) The Great Bath at Mohenjo-Daro and brick-built granaries. (5) Standardised weights and measures. (6) Trade contacts with Mesopotamia.

questions.question: Describe the political organisation of the Roman Republic.
questions.answer:
The Roman Republic (509-27 BCE) was governed by an elected aristocracy. Key institutions:
 - Two CONSULS, elected annually, headed the executive; each could veto the other.
 - The SENATE, made up of former magistrates, advised on policy and managed foreign affairs.
 - ASSEMBLIES of citizens elected magistrates and passed laws.
 - TRIBUNES of the plebs protected commoners' rights.
Elected magistrates held office for fixed terms; a complex web of checks and balances prevented any one person from accumulating absolute power. The system was, however, dominated in practice by wealthy patricians and later by powerful military leaders, ultimately collapsing into civil war and the Empire.

questions.question: Name three Greek philosophers and three Roman achievements.
questions.answer: Three Greek philosophers: Socrates, Plato and Aristotle (in chronological order, each taught the next). Three Roman achievements: (1) ROMAN LAW — basis of modern civil-law systems; (2) ROAD AND AQUEDUCT engineering — Appian Way, Pont du Gard; (3) The LATIN LANGUAGE — ancestor of the Romance languages.

questions.question: Name three features of the Achaemenid Persian Empire.
questions.answer: (1) Largest empire of the ancient world before Rome, spanning from Greece to the Indus. (2) Multi-ethnic administration via provinces (satrapies) under satraps. (3) The 'Royal Road' (Sardis to Susa) and a postal system enabled rapid communication. (4) Religious tolerance, including the famous edict of Cyrus permitting Jews to return to Jerusalem. (5) Zoroastrianism was the state religion.

questions.question: Describe how Buddhism and Jainism challenged Vedic Brahmanism.
questions.answer:
By the 6th century BCE, Vedic Brahmanism had become heavily ritualistic and dominated by priests. Buddhism and Jainism arose as critiques:
 - Both REJECTED elaborate ritual and animal sacrifice.
 - Both spoke in PRAKRIT or PALI (people's languages), not just Sanskrit.
 - Both opened spiritual practice to all CASTES, including the lowest.
 - Buddhism taught the Middle Way and the Four Noble Truths — practical psychology of suffering and its cessation.
 - Jainism emphasised AHIMSA (non-violence) in the strictest form, austerity, and respect for all life.
By speaking directly to common people in their own languages, opening the path to all, and rejecting expensive rituals, they offered an accessible alternative — and grew rapidly in north India.

questions.question: Describe the achievements of Ashoka.
questions.answer: Ashoka (~268-232 BCE) was the third Mauryan emperor and the most famous. His achievements include: (1) ruling the largest empire in ancient Indian history; (2) converting to BUDDHISM after the bloody Kalinga war and renouncing further military conquest; (3) inscribing his ROCK AND PILLAR EDICTS in Brahmi and other scripts across the empire, spreading messages of dharma, non-violence, tolerance and ethical conduct; (4) public welfare measures — building hospitals (for humans and animals), wells, roads, and rest-houses for travellers; (5) sending Buddhist missionaries — including his son Mahinda — to Sri Lanka, Burma and the Hellenistic world, spreading Buddhism beyond India. He is remembered as a model of ethical governance.

questions.question: List four major contributions of ancient India to world civilisation.
questions.answer:
(1) The DECIMAL PLACE-VALUE NOTATION and the concept of ZERO (Aryabhata, Brahmagupta) — the foundation of modern arithmetic.
(2) AYURVEDA — Charaka Samhita on medicine, Sushruta Samhita on surgery.
(3) The Sanskrit GRAMMAR of Panini, one of the most rigorous grammars ever composed.
(4) PHILOSOPHY — the six classical schools and the Upanishads.
Others: temple architecture, the Iron Pillar of Delhi, the cave art of Ajanta and Ellora, Kalidasa's plays and poetry, the Mahabharata and Ramayana.

questions.question: Why is the invention of zero so important to mathematics and science?
questions.answer: Zero is essential as BOTH a digit (place-holder) AND a number (an arithmetic quantity). As a digit, it makes the place-value system work — '105' means 1 hundred, 0 tens, 5 ones. As a number, it permits subtraction (5 − 5 = 0), the definition of negative numbers, and the algebraic equations that underlie all higher mathematics. Without zero, calculation is awkward (Roman numerals are notoriously hard to add) and many fields — algebra, calculus, computer science — would never have developed. The Indian invention of zero, transmitted through Arab mathematicians to medieval Europe, made the scientific revolution possible.

questions.question: Who was Alexander the Great and how far east did his conquests reach?
questions.answer: Alexander (356-323 BCE) was king of Macedon and one of the greatest military commanders in history. Educated by Aristotle, he ascended to the throne at age 20 and led the Macedonian–Greek army to conquer the Achaemenid Persian Empire. His conquests reached as far east as the INDUS RIVER, where he fought the Indian king Porus (Battle of the Hydaspes, 326 BCE). His army refused to go further east and he turned back. His campaigns spread Greek culture across an enormous area — leading to the 'Hellenistic age' across the eastern Mediterranean and Central Asia.

questions.question: Why did the earliest civilisations grow along great rivers?
questions.answer:
Three key reasons:
(1) FERTILE SOIL — annual flooding deposited rich silt, making agriculture productive. The Nile's flooding in particular reliably renewed Egypt's farmland.
(2) WATER for irrigation, drinking and domestic use — essential in otherwise dry regions.
(3) TRANSPORT — rivers were the highways of the ancient world. Boats moved grain, building materials and people far more cheaply than overland carriage. The river also linked settlements into a network of trade and communication.
Further: the predictability of seasonal flooding encouraged systematic record-keeping (calendars), which contributed to the development of writing and mathematics.

questions.question: Why is Athenian democracy considered an experiment, and what were its main strengths and limitations?
What were the main features of the Gupta classical age in India?
questions.answer: The Gupta empire (320-550 CE) is called India's 'classical age' for these features: (1) extended peace and prosperity across much of north India; (2) flourishing of art and literature — Kalidasa's plays, the formalisation of temple architecture; (3) advances in mathematics and astronomy (Aryabhata; rotation of the earth; π); (4) the development of decimal notation and zero; (5) a sophisticated administrative system; (6) tolerant religious environment — Hinduism revived, Buddhism flourished, Jainism continued.

questions.question: Name three significant scientific or technical achievements of ancient India.
questions.answer: (1) ZERO and the decimal place-value system (Aryabhata, Brahmagupta) — foundation of modern arithmetic. (2) Aryabhata's work in ASTRONOMY — accurate value of π, calculation of the length of the year, proposal that the earth rotates on its axis. (3) AYURVEDIC MEDICINE — Charaka and Sushruta's compilations; surgical techniques including plastic surgery; classification of diseases. Also: the IRON PILLAR of Delhi (metallurgy), and PANINI's grammar (linguistics).

questions.question: Tabulate the major contributions of Greek, Roman, Persian and Indian ancient civilisations in (a) governance, (b) law, (c) science / mathematics, (d) literature and arts.
questions.answer:
Civilisation  Governance               Law                       Science / Maths                    Literature & Arts
  Greek         Polis, democracy         Solon's & Drakon's codes  Pythagoras, Euclid, Archimedes    Sophocles, Homer, sculpture
  Roman         Republic + Empire        Codified Roman law         Engineering (aqueducts)            Latin literature, mosaics
  Persian       Satrapies, royal road    Religious tolerance edicts Royal postal system               Persepolis art, Avestan texts
  Indian        Mauryan + Gupta empires  Arthashastra; Manusmriti  Zero, π, sine; Ayurveda; metallurgy  Mahabharata, Ramayana, Kalidasa, cave temples

questions.question: Trace the progression of ancient Indian history from the Indus Valley civilisation to the Gupta empire.
questions.answer:
1. INDUS VALLEY (~2600-1900 BCE) — sophisticated urban civilisation along the Indus and its tributaries; planned cities of Mohenjo-Daro and Harappa; declined for reasons still debated (climate change, river shifts, possibly migration).

2. VEDIC AGE (~1500-500 BCE) — composition of the Vedas, spread of Sanskrit, gradual settlement of the Indo-Gangetic plain by Indo-Aryan speakers. By the late Vedic period, the social order organised into varnas, and small kingdoms emerged.

3. MAHAJANAPADAS (~600-300 BCE) — sixteen great kingdoms and oligarchic republics in north India; Magadha rose to dominate. Iron Age technology brought larger surpluses and bigger armies. Buddhism and Jainism arose as reformatory movements in the 6th century BCE.

4. MAURYAN EMPIRE (322-185 BCE) — Chandragupta unified most of the subcontinent; Ashoka (~268-232 BCE) brought ethical governance, Buddhism's spread, and the famous edicts.

5. POST-MAURYAN AGE (~185 BCE - 320 CE) — regional kingdoms; Indo-Greek, Shaka, Kushan dynasties; Sangam age in the south.

6. GUPTA EMPIRE (320-550 CE) — India's 'classical age'; flowering of mathematics (zero), astronomy (Aryabhata), literature (Kalidasa), art and temple architecture.

questions.question: Why is India described as having made 'tremendous contributions' to human civilisation? Give specific examples from at least five fields.
questions.answer:
India's contributions to world civilisation span many fields:

1. MATHEMATICS — the DECIMAL PLACE-VALUE SYSTEM and the concept of ZERO (Brahmagupta, 7th century CE) revolutionised arithmetic. Indian numerals spread westward as 'Arabic numerals' and underpin all modern calculation. Aryabhata's work on π, sine tables and algebra.

2. ASTRONOMY — Aryabhata proposed the earth's rotation on its axis (~5th century CE); calculated the length of the solar year to remarkable accuracy; explained eclipses by the earth's shadow on the moon.

3. MEDICINE — Ayurveda, with the Charaka Samhita (internal medicine) and Sushruta Samhita (surgery) as foundational texts; Sushruta described over 300 surgical procedures, including cataract surgery and plastic-surgery skin grafts.

4. METALLURGY — the Iron Pillar of Delhi (4th-5th century CE) has stood for over 1600 years without rusting; wootz steel (Indian crucible steel) was prized across the ancient world for its quality.

5. PHILOSOPHY — six classical schools (Sankhya, Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Mimamsa, Vedanta); the Upanishads; Buddhist and Jain philosophical traditions.

6. LITERATURE — the Mahabharata and Ramayana epics; Panini's Ashtadhyayi (Sanskrit grammar, ~5th century BCE — one of the most rigorous grammars ever composed); Kalidasa's plays and poems (Gupta age).

7. ART AND ARCHITECTURE — the Sanchi stupa; cave temples of Ajanta and Ellora; the diverse traditions of temple architecture.

These contributions, spread through trade and translation, profoundly influenced the Islamic world, China, Southeast Asia and (via Arab intermediaries) medieval Europe.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Around 10 000 BCE, in several places independently, people began to domesticate plants and animals. They settled in one place, built villages, made pottery and polished stone tools. This change is called the Neolithic revolution.

(i) What was the chief technological change at the start of the Neolithic?
(ii) How did the Neolithic revolution affect human settlement patterns?
(iii) Why is it called a 'revolution' even though it took thousands of years?
(iv) What downstream developments did it eventually make possible?
questions.answer:
(i) The shift from hunting and gathering to AGRICULTURE — domesticating wild plants and animals and producing food deliberately. Polished stone tools, pottery and weaving accompanied this shift.
(ii) People moved from nomadic, small bands following game herds to PERMANENT VILLAGES near their farms — the first stable, dense settlements.
(iii) Although the change took millennia to spread worldwide, its CONSEQUENCES were so transformative — population growth, accumulation of property, social hierarchies, larger settlements — that historians call it revolutionary in the long-arc sense. It changed everything about how humans live.
(iv) The food SURPLUS made possible: specialisation of labour (some people could become priests, craftsmen, soldiers); WRITING (to keep records); RELIGION and centralised administration; and ultimately CITIES, KINGDOMS and CIVILISATION itself.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The Indus Valley Civilisation (~2600-1900 BCE) had planned cities, sophisticated drainage, weights and measures, and trade contacts with Mesopotamia. Mohenjo-Daro had the Great Bath, a large public tank.

(i) Where (modern country) did the Indus Valley civilisation flourish?
(ii) Name two famous cities.
(iii) Why is the Indus civilisation called 'highly developed' for its time?
(iv) What is one mystery about the Indus civilisation that remains unsolved?
questions.answer:
(i) Mostly in modern PAKISTAN, with sites in north-western INDIA (Gujarat, Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana).
(ii) Mohenjo-Daro and Harappa (others: Dholavira, Lothal, Kalibangan, Rakhigarhi).
(iii) Highly developed because: planned cities with grid streets, brick-built houses, the world's earliest known SEWERS and covered drains, standardised weights and measures, a writing system (undeciphered), public buildings (Great Bath, granaries), seal-making and metallurgy, and long-distance TRADE with Mesopotamia.
(iv) Two famous mysteries: (a) the HARAPPAN SCRIPT remains UNDECIPHERED — we cannot read what the Indus people wrote; (b) the CAUSE OF DECLINE is debated — possibilities include climate change, drying of the Saraswati / Ghaggar-Hakra river system, river course shifts, internal social changes, or migration.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Athens introduced democracy around 500 BCE — citizens met in the Assembly and voted on laws. But citizenship was restricted to free adult males of Athenian parentage. Women, slaves and resident foreigners were excluded.

(i) What was unprecedented about Athenian democracy?
(ii) Who could and could not vote?
(iii) Is it correct to call Athens a democracy in the modern sense?
(iv) What legacy does Athenian democracy leave for the world?
questions.answer:
(i) Unprecedented: ordinary CITIZENS gathered in person to vote on laws, judge cases and elect (or sort by lot) magistrates. No king or aristocracy held final authority — the demos (people) did.
(ii) Could vote: free adult males of Athenian parentage (perhaps 30 000 out of a population of 250 000). Could NOT vote: women, slaves, resident foreigners (metics), children.
(iii) Not in the modern sense — modern democracy is universal-suffrage based and representative. Athenian democracy excluded the majority of residents and was direct rather than representative. But it was a DEMOCRACY in the strict etymological sense (rule by demos), and a vital experiment.
(iv) Athenian democracy left an enduring legacy: the IDEA that citizens can govern themselves; the institutions of public assembly, jury trial, term limits and accountability; the words 'democracy', 'politics' and 'citizen'; and the inspiration for all later democratic experiments — including modern parliamentary and constitutional democracies.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Rome went from a small city (founded ~753 BCE) to a Republic (509 BCE) to an Empire (27 BCE under Augustus). At its peak it ruled from Britain to the Persian Gulf.

(i) Name the three phases of Rome's political development.
(ii) Who was the first Roman emperor?
(iii) State two enduring contributions of Rome.
(iv) What event in the 5th century CE is conventionally called the end of the Western Roman Empire?
questions.answer:
(i) MONARCHY (753-509 BCE, traditional dates); REPUBLIC (509-27 BCE); EMPIRE (27 BCE - 476 CE in the West; the Eastern / Byzantine half continued until 1453 CE).
(ii) Augustus (originally named Octavian), in 27 BCE — the adopted son of Julius Caesar.
(iii) (a) ROMAN LAW — the foundation of modern civil-law systems across Europe and Latin America. (b) ROMAN ENGINEERING — aqueducts, roads (some still in use), arches, concrete, the dome. Bonus: Latin language → Romance languages; Christianity transmitted as the state religion.
(iv) The deposition of the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, by the Germanic leader Odoacer in 476 CE, is conventionally taken as the end of the Western Roman Empire.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In the 6th century BCE, two reformatory movements arose in India: Buddhism (founded by Gautama Buddha) and Jainism (founded by Mahavira). Both rejected elaborate ritual and emphasised personal ethical conduct.

(i) Who founded each religion?
(ii) State two principles common to both Buddhism and Jainism.
(iii) State one difference between Buddhism and Jainism.
(iv) Why did both spread widely among common people?
questions.answer:
(i) Buddhism — Gautama Buddha. Jainism — Mahavira (Vardhamana).
(ii) Common principles: (a) AHIMSA (non-violence) — neither religion permits the killing of living beings. (b) REJECTION of priestly authority and elaborate ritual. (c) Both opened spiritual practice to all CASTES — universalist, not exclusively for Brahmins.
(iii) Differences: Jainism is much STRICTER about ahimsa (Jain monks sweep the path before them to avoid stepping on insects); Buddhism teaches the MIDDLE WAY (avoiding both indulgence and extreme austerity), whereas Jainism stresses austerity / penance more. Also: Buddhism became a major world religion (China, Japan, SE Asia); Jainism remained largely Indian.
(iv) Both spread widely because they: (a) spoke in PRAKRIT / PALI (people's tongues), not just Sanskrit; (b) admitted all castes; (c) addressed the practical problem of suffering and how to escape it; (d) avoided expensive rituals that only the wealthy could afford. They offered an accessible spiritual path that ordinary people could understand and follow.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Ashoka was the third Mauryan emperor (~268-232 BCE). After the bloody Kalinga war, in which thousands were killed, he was so disturbed that he renounced military conquest and converted to Buddhism.

(i) Which battle changed Ashoka's life?
(ii) Which religion did Ashoka adopt?
(iii) How did Ashoka spread his new principles across the empire?
(iv) Name two welfare measures Ashoka introduced.
questions.answer:
(i) The KALINGA war (~261 BCE) — Ashoka's conquest of the kingdom of Kalinga (modern Odisha) was unusually bloody, with reported deaths in the lakhs.
(ii) BUDDHISM.
(iii) Through ROCK AND PILLAR EDICTS — inscriptions in Brahmi and other scripts, placed across the empire (and even beyond, e.g. in modern-day Afghanistan). They taught DHARMA — non-violence, religious tolerance, respect for elders, kind treatment of servants and animals. He also sent Buddhist missionaries to Sri Lanka, Burma and the Hellenistic kingdoms.
(iv) (a) Built HOSPITALS for both humans and animals. (b) Constructed wells, rest-houses and shade-trees along roads for travellers. (c) Promoted environmental measures — protected animals from slaughter, planted medicinal herbs.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The number system 1, 2, 3, ..., 9, 0 is called 'Arabic' in English but actually originated in India. Indian mathematicians (Aryabhata, Brahmagupta) developed the place-value notation and made zero a number in its own right.

(i) Why are these numerals called 'Arabic'?
(ii) What does 'place-value notation' mean?
(iii) Why is zero an important number?
(iv) How did the Indian system reach Europe?
questions.answer:
(i) Europeans first encountered the system through Arab mathematicians — particularly al-Khwarizmi, who wrote about Indian numerals in 9th-century Baghdad. The Latin scholars who imported the system from Arabic-speaking Spain called them 'Arabic numerals'. Arab scholars themselves correctly call them 'Hindu numerals'.
(ii) Place-value notation means the VALUE of a digit depends on its POSITION. In '305', the digit '3' means '3 hundreds' because it's in the hundreds position. This is far more compact than older systems (Roman, Greek, Egyptian) where each numeral has a fixed value (X always means 10).
(iii) Zero plays two roles: (a) as a digit, it's the PLACEHOLDER that makes positional notation work — without zero we couldn't write '305' distinctly from '35'. (b) as a NUMBER, it permits operations like subtraction (5 − 5 = 0) and enables algebra (where 0 is the additive identity). Brahmagupta gave the first systematic rules.
(iv) The Indian system reached the Arab world by the 9th century, then crossed into Latin Europe through translations made in Spain (especially Toledo) in the 12th-13th centuries. The Italian mathematician Fibonacci popularised it in his Liber Abaci (1202). Within a few centuries it had largely replaced Roman numerals across Europe.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The Achaemenid Persian Empire (550-330 BCE), founded by Cyrus the Great, was the largest empire of the ancient world before Rome. It stretched from Greece to the Indus and had multi-ethnic administration.

(i) Who founded the Achaemenid Persian Empire?
(ii) Across what geographic range did it stretch?
(iii) State two administrative innovations of the Persians.
(iv) Who finally defeated the Achaemenid Empire?
questions.answer:
(i) CYRUS THE GREAT — around 550 BCE, by uniting the Persians and overthrowing the Medes.
(ii) From the AEGEAN COAST of modern Turkey (and parts of Greece) in the west, across modern Iran, to the INDUS RIVER in the east — over 5 million square kilometres.
(iii) (a) SATRAPIES — the empire was divided into provinces, each governed by a satrap (governor) accountable to the king. (b) The ROYAL ROAD — over 2500 km long, linking Sardis to Susa, with a postal-relay system that delivered messages in days. Also: religious tolerance, multi-cultural administration, and standardised coinage.
(iv) ALEXANDER THE GREAT of Macedon, in a series of campaigns (334-330 BCE), defeated the last Achaemenid king Darius III and brought the empire to an end.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Greek civilisation made significant contributions in philosophy, drama, mathematics and architecture. Roman civilisation contributed law, engineering and the Latin language.

(i) Name three Greek philosophers (in the order one taught the next).
(ii) Name one Greek mathematician and his contribution.
(iii) Why is Roman law important to the modern world?
(iv) Name three modern languages descended from Latin.
questions.answer:
(i) SOCRATES → PLATO → ARISTOTLE. (Plato was Socrates's student; Aristotle was Plato's. Aristotle in turn tutored Alexander the Great.)
(ii) Examples: PYTHAGORAS (the Pythagorean theorem about right-angled triangles); EUCLID (Elements — the foundation of geometry); ARCHIMEDES (lever law, principle of buoyancy, value of π).
(iii) Roman law was the first attempt at a comprehensive, secular CODIFIED legal system. Concepts like property, contract, citizenship, trust, and the distinction between civil and criminal law all have Roman roots. The civil-law systems of continental Europe (and, by extension, Latin America, Quebec, much of Africa and parts of Asia) are direct descendants. Common-law systems (UK, USA, India) also borrowed extensively.
(iv) ITALIAN, FRENCH, SPANISH (also PORTUGUESE, ROMANIAN, CATALAN). All called 'Romance languages' — from Roma (Rome) via Latin.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The Gupta empire (320-550 CE) is often called the 'classical age' of India. It saw advances in mathematics (Aryabhata), literature (Kalidasa), art and temple architecture.

(i) What is the period of the Gupta empire?
(ii) Why is it called India's 'classical age'?
(iii) Name one mathematician and one poet of this era.
(iv) How long did the Gupta empire last?
questions.answer:
(i) Approximately 320 CE to 550 CE — about two and a quarter centuries.
(ii) Because of the FLOWERING of culture, science, art and learning: extensive peace, prosperity, religious tolerance, the development of decimal mathematics and the formal positing of zero, advances in astronomy, the formalisation of temple architecture, and the great Sanskrit literature of the era. The era set 'classical' standards in many fields that later Indians looked back to as a model.
(iii) Mathematician: ARYABHATA (proposed the rotation of the earth, accurate value of π). Poet/playwright: KALIDASA (Shakuntala, Meghaduta, Raghuvansham).
(iv) Roughly 230 years (320 CE to 550 CE). After 550 CE the empire fragmented into smaller successor kingdoms.
